title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Introduction
content: The oculomotor nerve (the third cranial nerve) carries 3 primary motor functions: it provides parasympathetic innervation to the pupil and lens for pupillary constriction and accommodation, supplies somatic motor innervation to the levator palpebrae superioris muscle to elevate the upper eyelid, and innervates most of the extraocular muscles responsible for visual tracking and gaze fixation. Like other nerve fibers in the human body, the oculomotor nerve can be impaired by disease, leading to lifelong impairment of normal vision. Dysfunction can also be indicative of more serious underlying diseases, such as an aneurysm or a neoplasm.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Structure and Function
content: The oculomotor nerve originates from 2 nuclei in the midbrain: the oculomotor nucleus and the accessory parasympathetic nucleus (Edinger-Westphal nucleus). [1] The oculomotor nerve exits the brainstem near midline at the base of the midbrain just caudal to the mammillary bodies. It passes through the cavernous sinus and proceeds through the supraorbital fissure to reach the orbit of the eye (Figure 1). The oculomotor nerve has both somatic and autonomic fibers. Somatic (voluntary) nerve fibers are bundled deep inside the nerve, while the autonomic (involuntary) fibers surround the somatic fibers around the outside of the nerve. Knowing the spatial layout of these fibers help one understand the various forms of presentation in third nerve palsies.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Structure and Function
content: The somatic (voluntary) functions of the oculomotor nerve include elevation of the upper eyelid through innervation of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle, as well as coordination of several extraocular muscles responsible for visual tracking and gaze fixation. These eye movements are mediated by 4 muscles innervated by the oculomotor nerve. The superior rectus elevates the eye from the primary (straight-ahead) position. The medial rectus adducts the eye toward the nose from the primary position. The inferior rectus depresses the eye from the primary position. The inferior oblique elevates the eye when it is adducted from the primary position and also contributes to extorsion.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Structure and Function
content: There are 2 primary functions of the autonomic parasympathetic (involuntary) oculomotor nerve. It constricts the pupil (miosis) by innervating the smooth muscle (sphincter pupillae) near the pupil. It also innervates the ciliary muscles. These muscles connect the iris to the choroid. Contraction of the muscle alters the curvature of the lens, which allows individuals to focus the lens on near objects (see Figure. Oculomotor Nerve Palsy). [2]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Embryology
content: The oculomotor nerve and its associated cranial nerve nuclei exist within the midbrain. The midbrain develops from the mesencephalon. Neuroblasts from the basal plates develop into the tegmentum. The tegmentum includes the oculomotor and trochlear nerves, Edinger-Westphal nuclei, oculomotor nuclei, trochlear nuclei, red nuclei, and reticular nuclei. The occulomotor nerve has somatic and autonomic functions. Somatic nerves are homologous with the ventral roots of spinal nerves. They originate from the basal plate and innervate the superior rectus, inferior rectus, medial rectus, and inferior oblique muscles. These muscles derive from the first preoptic myotome.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Embryology
content: Most research about the development of parasympathetic nerves and the ciliary ganglion has been on chickens. The parasympathetic nerve supply of the oculomotor nerves develops from the caudal midbrain and rostral hindbrain neural crest cells. Some cells may also originate from the ectodermal placode caudal to the eye. [3] [4] These cells migrate ventrolaterally and rostrally toward the optic vesicle. As the neurons in the ciliary ganglion differentiate, they extend axons to innervate the blood vessels of the choroid plexus as well as the striated muscles of the iris and ciliary body. [5]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Blood Supply and Lymphatics
content: The somatic and autonomic components of the oculomotor nerve have differentiated vascular supplies. The vasa vasorum supplies the inner somatic (voluntary) nerve fibers, while the pia mater blood vessels supply the outer autonomic nerve fibers. [2] Lymphatic drainage of the orbit of the eye is not yet well understood. There is morphological evidence of lymphatic structures within the lacrimal gland and the arachnoid; however, distinctive lymphatic structures in other regions of the orbit are currently unknown. [6] Both the oculomotor nucleus and Edinger-Westphal nucleus are both located in the medial midbrain, which is supplied by the paramedian branches of the upper basilar artery and the proximal posterior cerebral artery.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Nerves
content: The oculomotor nerve helps to adjust and coordinate eye position during movement. Several movements assist with this process: saccades, smooth pursuit, fixation, accommodation, vestibulo-ocular reflex, and optokinetic reflex. Saccades are rapid, jerky motions of the eye. This type of motion typically occurs when moving the gaze between objects. When tracking an object, we use smooth pursuit to keep our eyes on it as it moves. When we want to stare at an object, we fixate on that object. Control of each of these actions is by either vestibule-ocular or optokinetic reflexes. The vestibulo-ocular reflex adjusts eye position during rapid head movements. Head motion activates cells within the semicircular canals. Information about the motion is transmitted to the ipsilateral vestibular nucleus and forwarded to the oculomotor nucleus. Therefore, if the head moves to the left, the eyes move to the right to maintain a steady gaze.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Nerves
content: The optokinetic reflex adjusts eye position in response to changes in the visual field. This reflex initiates from visual information. Information about the visual field is transmitted from the parieto-occipital eye field through the pontine nuclei to the vestibulo-cerebellum. It then moves through the vestibular nuclei to the oculomotor nucleus, where eye movement initiates. This reflex allows the eyes to follow large objects in the visual field. The last action is accommodation. This action helps to keep the gaze focused when both vestibular and visual stimuli change. It requires interaction between the vestibulo-ocular and optokinetic reflexes. [7] [8] Deficits within the peripheral or central vestibular system result in inappropriate, rapid eye movement, “nystagmus.” The direction of the fast phase of nystagmus can assist clinicians in diagnosing a patient’s pathology.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Muscles
content: The oculomotor nerve provides motor innervation to multiple extraocular and intraocular structures essential for eyelid elevation, ocular alignment, and near vision. It innervates the levator palpebrae superioris, which elevates the upper eyelid. Among the extraocular muscles, it supplies the superior rectus, which elevates the eye; the medial rectus, which adducts the eye toward the nose; the inferior rectus, which depresses the eye; and the inferior oblique, which contributes to elevation and extorsion of the eye when it is adducted. The oculomotor nerve also carries parasympathetic fibers to the intrinsic muscles of the eye. These fibers innervate the ciliary muscle, which adjusts lens curvature for near accommodation, and the sphincter pupillae, which constricts the pupil in response to light and during near focus.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Muscles
content: Motor control of the remaining extraocular muscles is supplied by the trochlear and abducens nerves. The trochlear nerve (fourth cranial nerve) innervates the superior oblique muscle, which primarily depresses and intorts the eye, especially when it is adducted. The abducens nerve (sixth cranial nerve) innervates the lateral rectus muscle, which abducts the eye, moving it laterally toward the ear on the same side.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Physiologic Variants
content: Congenital oculomotor palsy is a rare condition that is typically caused by increased intracranial pressure at the junction between the posterior communicating artery and the internal carotid artery, which causes a local compression of the oculomotor nerve. Symptoms of this disorder include a unilaterally fixed pupil size that is unreactive to light. Additional symptoms include unilateral ptosis and decreased visual acuity. While oculomotor palsy is not life-threatening, the presence at birth may be a sign of other congenital malformations (eg, PHACE syndrome, type 2 neurofibromatosis, and Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome). Even in the absence of other neurological signs, clinicians should examine these patients for more significant malformations. [9]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Surgical Considerations
content: One of the main goals of intracranial neurosurgery should be to avoid postsurgical complications. A dilated pupil and ptosis are the most common clinical presentations of oculomotor nerve palsy post-neurosurgery, usually after clipping of an intracranial aneurysm. [10] Patients who undergo open surgery or a minimally invasive technique on basilar artery aneurysms may develop a third nerve palsy after surgery, although this complication has been shown to be transient. [11]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Clinical Significance
content: Recognizing oculomotor nerve dysfunction (oculomotor nerve palsy) is crucial because it can be a sign of underlying or uncontrolled chronic disease states. It is an essential clinical symptom that can be life-saving in certain circumstances.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Clinical Significance -- Pathophysiology
content: The cause of oculomotor nerve palsy is most commonly due to microvascular diseases, including diabetes, hypertension, compression from an intracranial neoplasm or an aneurysm, or trauma. [10] The microvascular disease can affect the vasa vasorum. In these instances, the fibers innervating the upper eyelid and most of the extraocular muscles become ischemic. Compression of the oculomotor nerve can also occur via an aneurysm, intracranial neoplasm, or uncal herniation. These ischemic events can affect the outer pia blood vessels supplying the fibers to the pupil and lens and eventually the inner vasa vasorum.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Clinical Significance -- Clinical Signs
content: An oculomotor nerve palsy produces a characteristic clinical pattern due to loss of both somatic motor and parasympathetic function. Ptosis is common and results from paralysis of the levator palpebrae superioris muscle. The affected eye typically assumes a “down and out” position due to the unopposed action of the lateral rectus muscle (innervated by the abducens nerve), which abducts the eye, and the superior oblique muscle (innervated by the trochlear nerve), which depresses and intorts the eye when adducted. Diplopia occurs because of ocular misalignment; however, it may not be reported if significant ptosis obstructs vision in the affected eye. A dilated pupil may be present if parasympathetic fibers are involved, reflecting loss of sphincter pupillae function. In such cases, the affected pupil fails to constrict appropriately during direct or consensual light testing. On the swinging flashlight test, illumination of either eye not produce constriction in the affected pupil if parasympathetic efferent function is impaired. Loss of accommodation can also occur due to paralysis of the ciliary muscle. This finding may be difficult to assess in older adults, as age-related lens stiffening (presbyopia) can independently reduce accommodative ability.

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Clinical Significance -- Labs and Imaging
content: Evaluation of suspected oculomotor nerve palsy should be guided primarily by the presence or absence of pupil involvement, as this distinction has important diagnostic implications. If the pupil is spared, a microvascular ischemic etiology is more likely, particularly in patients with vascular risk factors. In these cases, evaluation should include blood pressure measurement, hemoglobin A1c testing, a complete blood count, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate to assess for diabetes, hypertension, anemia, or inflammatory conditions. If the pupil is involved, a compressive lesion must be suspected until proven otherwise. This warrants urgent referral to a neuro-ophthalmologist and prompt neuroimaging. Magnetic resonance imaging should be obtained, and computed tomography angiography is indicated if an intracranial aneurysm, particularly of the posterior communicating artery, is suspected. [2]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Clinical Significance -- Conservative Management
content: Treatment is conservative in the acute phase. If diplopia is present and distressful, an eye patch, opaque contact lens, or a blurred lens in glasses covering the affected eye can be helpful. Botulinum toxin can be useful in the acute setting of partial third nerve palsy with horizontal deviation; it is best used when paralysis is limited to the medial rectus. In these cases, injection into the overcompensating lateral rectus corrects horizontal deviation in the primary position. If mild vertical deviation remains, prisms in glasses may be helpful. Botulinum toxin should be avoided in cases of vertical muscle imbalance due to the high complication rate. [12] Most patients (63%) with an acquired third nerve palsy recover completely with conservative management. Patients with microvascular etiology have the greatest chance of full recovery. [10]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Clinical Significance -- Surgical management
content: Minimal or no improvement after 6 months of appropriate conservative management is an indication to consider strabismus surgery. The goal of surgery is to correct ocular misalignment by adjusting the tension and position of the extraocular muscles. Two primary techniques are used. A recession involves detaching the muscle from its insertion and reattaching it posteriorly on the globe to weaken its action. A resection involves removing a segment of the muscle and reattaching it to effectively shorten and strengthen its pull. Depending on the pattern of deviation, the surgeon typically recesses the overacting or contracted muscle and resects its antagonist to restore balanced alignment. [12] If the pupil is involved, patients should undergo a thorough evaluation by a neurologist. [2]

title: Neuroanatomy, Cranial Nerve 3 (Oculomotor) -- Other Issues
content: As individuals age, it is common to lose near-focusing ability (presbyopia). In these individuals, the ciliary muscle contracts when stimulated. However, the muscle's physical characteristics will show differences that correlate with the presbyopia deficit. Researchers report that in such cases, the muscle is shorter and the internal apical edge moves forward. These results suggest that changes in the muscle, rather than changes in its innervation, may account for presbyopia. [13]
